title: Agent Desk
subtitle: Making two opposing metrics win at once — speed and compliance — in a high-stakes fintech workflow

indexedSections.title: Human middleware, at 3.2 days per application

value: ==Agent Desk is Best Egg's internal platform where verification agents approve or reject credit applications — personal loans, credit cards, and secured auto loans== — inside fraud-prevention and compliance rules. The decisions are irreversible, and they land on real people's credit outcomes.

The legacy system was fragmented across agent roles, forcing agents to act as "human middleware" — a 3.2-day bottleneck per application. As the solo designer, I owned it end-to-end: the workflow, the UX success metrics, and shipping inside a heavily regulated environment.

items.label: Constraint 1
items.title: Speed vs. compliance
items.desc: Workflows had to move faster without compromising fraud prevention, regulation, or auditability.

items.label: Constraint 2
items.title: Multiple agent roles
items.desc: Different agent types needed different access and authority in the same workflow.

items.label: Constraint 3
items.title: Irreversible decisions
items.desc: Agents made frequent irreversible calls under time pressure — fatigue and error risk compounded.

indexedSections.title: Two metrics that fight each other

items.label: Business wanted speed
items.desc: A single application took 3.2 days — a massive bottleneck.

items.label: Risk wanted rigor
items.desc: Verification rate sat at ~80% — too many valid applications weren't clearing.

value: The trap: these metrics are naturally opposed. Push agents faster and they get sloppy — verification rate drops. Tell them to slow down and time climbs. Most teams pick one.

blocks.label: The harder brief
blocks.value: Can both opposing metrics improve at once? That ruled out brute force — more people, more time — and forced the solution to come from design decisions themselves.

indexedSections.title: Four decisions that broke the tradeoff

blocks.title: ==Find the real bottleneck (it wasn't a screen)==

value: With no researcher and a lean team, I used the lowest-cost, highest-signal method: live agent shadowing. Sitting beside agents on real cases, I watched them bounce across five or six systems — the legacy Agent Desktop, the Admin console, LoanPro, LexisNexis, raw spreadsheets — cross-checking the same data by hand, on tribal knowledge, with no single source of truth.

blocks.label: The legacy reality — one verification, five systems

value: I mapped the journey across five stages — Triage, Review & Verification, Investigation, Decision & Documentation, Outcome — and the emotional low points lined up exactly with the system gaps: overwhelmed at review, distracted mid-investigation, anxious at close-out, never sure what the scattered data had hidden.

blocks.label: Five-stage journey map — emotion curve, verbatim quotes, and the design response per stage
The insight
blocks.value: The 3.2 days weren't lost inside any one screen — they were lost in the gaps between systems. Agents were human middleware, reconciling data by hand.

value: So my first decision wasn't "make a page prettier." It was eliminate the middleware — consolidating scattered tools and data into one workspace: centralized application management across loan and card products, plus a Manager's Menu holding the customer data agents kept leaving for.

Here I hit a hard constraint. Cognitive load was brutal, but I couldn't cut information to reduce it: compliance requires every data point needed for verification to stay visible, and removing any risks the audit trail.
So the decision became: reduce load through structure, not subtraction.

items.title: Left–right split
items.desc: Mapped to the agent's mental model: data to read on the left, actions to take on the right — making "read, then decide" legible in space.

items.title: Verification Checklist & Clear CTAs
items.desc: Tribal rules made explicit — steps auto-resolve to "Clear" as they complete, and critical actions sit predictably at the end.

items.title: Notes & History, always in view
items.desc: Persistent notes and instant access to previous records, so context is never re-fetched from another system.

items.title: Verification Checklist
items.desc: Every verification step consolidated and aligned with business rules, updating in real time and auto-resolving to "Clear".

items.title: Notes & History
items.desc: Always-visible note entry and access to previous records support informed decision-making.

value: Same information, zero removed — but the structure now carried the attention, serving speed and accuracy at once. And because the layout is structural rather than role-specific, the same logic held across every agent role: one mental model, many permission levels.

blocks.title: ==Design the right friction for irreversible actions==

value: Every agent click is irreversible — an approval or rejection deciding a real person's credit outcome, with compliance weight.
Auto-resolving checklist items felt great, but over-automation risks complacency — agents blindly trusting the system. So I drew a line:

blocks.label: The line
blocks.value: Objective, checkable items auto-clear. Anything needing human judgment must be confirmed by the agent.

value: I also added a Preview/Edit mode — a final review before submission. On the surface it adds a step and fights the speed goal. My argument: in irreversible decisions, the rework a preview prevents is worth far more than the two seconds it costs. Slowing this one step makes the whole flow faster.
That's friction in the right place, inside compliance lines that forbid one-click batch actions or skipped steps.

items.title: Centralized Application Management
items.desc: Loan and credit card applications in one workspace, with proactive alerts for data issues.

blocks.value: Preview/Edit only works if the agent actually reads it — nothing forces attention, only presence. It lowers the error rate; it doesn't zero it.

blocks.title: ==Grant access by role, not by default==

value: The Manager's Menu applied decision one's consolidation logic to the manager tier. That raised a harder question than "what's in the workspace": should every agent see everything in it? Compliance said no. Different agent types carry different decision authority, and access has to match it exactly.

So I designed permissions as a first-class layer of the workspace, not a settings-page afterthought. Junior agents get the baseline — application data, checklist, notes. Managers layer the Manager's Menu on top: cross-account visibility, override authority, and the tools to unblock a case an agent can't resolve. Same interface, different ceiling.

items.title: Manager's Menu
items.desc: Comprehensive access to customer data, reducing the need for external tools.

blocks.value: Role boundaries were set with Compliance, not measured — there's no dataset proving the right cutoff between agent and manager access, only a defensible one.

items.label: Agent confidence & satisfaction
items.desc: Reported post-launch, against the pre-defined UX metric

value: The MVP launch drew strong feedback from agents and leadership, with higher reported confidence and satisfaction.

Crucially, the two opposing metrics improved together, with distinct drivers: the unified workspace and explicit checklist removed cross-system shuttling (speed), while Preview/Edit and role-scoped access reduced misjudgment (verification rate).

blocks.value: Agent Desk 3.0 is a major leap forward in our verification process — transforming how agents work and unlocking better customer experiences.
